elements.text: Topic: Binary to Decimal Conversion for IPv4
Good morning, Roosevelt! Today is Friday, October 23, 2026. Let's start fresh with a vital building block for your November 9th exam.

segments.speech: Good morning, Roosevelt! Rise and shine! It's Friday morning, and your exam is coming up on November 9th. Today, we are going to master IPv4 Address Conversions, starting from the absolute ground up. Let's get right into it!

elements.text: An IPv4 address is like a mailing address for a device on a network. It consists of 32 bits, divided into 4 octets of 8 bits each.

segments.speech: Think of an IPv4 address like a house address. Just like your house needs a street name and house number so mail can find you, a computer needs an IP address to receive data on a network. Each address is made of 32 bits, split into four groups called octets. Does that make sense so far, Roosevelt?

elements.text: An IPv4 address is written as four numbers separated by dots, like 192.168.1.1. Each of these four numbers is called an 'octet' because it represents 8 binary bits.

segments.speech: To break this down further, Roosevelt, those 32 bits are grouped into four chunks called octets, separated by periods. Each octet has 8 bits. Does that grouping make sense so far?
